q: Per Sec. 6.4, which survey/data must the Owner furnish (or have the Architect obtain, at the Owner's expense)?
o: A certified survey of the site (topographical/relocation surveys, boundaries, utility lines, soil investigations, etc.)
The Architect's professional indemnity insurance
The building permit application form only
The Contractor's performance bond
n: Sec. 6.4 requires the Owner to furnish or direct the Architect to obtain, at the Owner's expense, a certified survey of the site covering topographical/relocation data, boundaries, utility lines, zoning compliance, and soil investigations. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 6.4)

q: To what kind of work does the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses method of compensation (Sec. 5.2) apply exclusively, and for what reason?
o: Construction supervision work only
Purely creative design work, since it best rewards artistic talent
Non-creative work such as accounting, secretarial tasks, research, and data gathering — because creative design's value cannot be measured by time spent
Government projects exclusively
n: Sec. 5.2 states this cost-based method applies only to non-creative work (accounting, secretarial, research, data gathering, report preparation, etc.) since creative design's value cannot be measured by hours spent. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.2)

q: Per Sec. 2.5.2.a and Sec. 33 of R.A. No. 9266, who holds ownership over the Bid Documents used in a competitive bidding, and what may bidders be asked to post?
o: Ownership shifts to the government the moment a bid is submitted
The Architect keeps sole ownership and copyright; a bond may be required to guarantee the documents' return
The Owner keeps sole ownership; bidders retain the documents permanently once bidding opens
The winning Contractor owns the documents upon award; no bond applies
n: Sec. 2.5.2.a states the Bid Documents are the intellectual property of the Architect (Sec. 33, R.A. No. 9266) and must be returned; a bond may be required to assure their return. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 2.5.2.a)

q: A proposed public market and a warehouse are being classified under SPP Document 202's project categories. Which Group do they belong to?
o: Group 5 — monumental buildings
Group 3 — buildings of exceptional character and complexity
Group 1 — buildings of the simplest utilization and character
Group 2 — buildings of moderate complexity
n: Sec. 4.1 (Group 1) lists Public Markets and Warehouses among buildings of the simplest utilization and character. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 4.1)

q: Suppose the parties had instead agreed on the maximum multiplier allowed under Sec. 5.2 (2.5) rather than 2.0. What would the resulting Fee have been?
n: At the maximum allowable multiplier of 2.5, Fee = P62,000 x 2.5 = P155,000. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.2)
scenario: Architect Reyes takes on a small renovation job — non-creative, cost-based work — under the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses method (SPP Doc. 202, Sec. 5.2). Her own billing rate is P800/hour across 40 logged hours; her Consultant bills P600/hour for 20 hours; and her Technical Staff bills P300/hour for 60 hours. The parties settle on a multiplier (M) of 2.0 to cover overhead and profit, and reimbursable expenses (R) for the whole engagement come to P15,000.

q: Per Sec. 7.1, what is the Architect's Fee based on, and what follows if the Architect must render additional services?
o: The Fee rests on the Project Construction Cost; additional services call for additional compensation
Additional services are always absorbed within the original fee at no extra charge
The Fee is a fixed government-set amount, whatever services are rendered
The Fee is based solely on the Architect's years of experience
n: Sec. 7.1 states the Architect's Fee is based on the Project Construction Cost, and where the Architect renders additional services, additional compensation shall be required. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.1)

q: Which of these does NOT belong among the Architect's duties during the Contract Document Phase (Sec. 2.4)?
o: Preparing Technical Specifications describing the type and quality of materials and the manner of construction
Updating the SPPCC to reflect changes in scope, requirements, or market conditions
Awarding the construction contract to the winning bidder
Preparing complete Contract Documents comprising detailed designs and construction drawings
n: Awarding the construction contract occurs during the Bidding or Negotiation Phase (Sec. 2.5.1.b: "assists the Owner...to awarding of the construction contract"), not the Contract Document Phase, whose duties are described in Sec. 2.4.1, 2.4.2 and 2.4.4. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 2.4 and Sec. 2.5.1.b)

q: If a project calls for acoustic/illumination specialists, mural painters, or sculptors (Sec. 7.2), who puts these forward to the Owner, and what fee does the Architect collect?
o: The Contractor recommends them, and the Architect earns no added compensation
The PRBoA assigns them directly and bills the Owner
The Owner sources them on his own, with no Architect involvement or fee
The Architect recommends them for the Owner's approval and earns a coordination fee for these services, paid separately by the Owner
n: Sec. 7.2 states other services (acoustic/illumination specialists, mural painters, sculptors, etc.) are recommended by the Architect for the Owner's approval, paid for separately by the Owner, subject to a coordination fee payable to the Architect. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.2)

q: When the Owner requires specialist consultants, whose consent is needed to engage them under Sec. 7.9, and how does their cost relate to the Architect's own fee?
o: Engaged solely with the Contractor's consent
Engaged only with the PRBoA's prior approval, billed to the Architect
Engaged with the Architect's consent; their cost is paid separately by the Owner and is NOT deducted from the Architect's fee
Engaged without anyone's consent; their cost comes out of the Architect's fee
n: Sec. 7.9 requires specialist consultants to be engaged with the Architect's consent, with their cost paid separately by the Owner and not deducted from the Architect's fee. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.9)

q: During a routine periodic site visit, an Architect notices the Contractor's masonry work fails to match the Contract Documents. What must the Architect do under Sec. 2.6.3?
o: Personally terminate the Contractor's contract on the spot
Say nothing, since continuous supervision isn't required of the Architect
Pay for the corrective work from his own fee
Report the noted defects/deficiencies to the Client and condemn any work that fails to conform to the Contract Documents
n: Sec. 2.6.3 requires the Architect, on the basis of site-visit observations, to report defects/deficiencies to the Client and condemn work failing to conform to the Contract Documents. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 2.6.3)

q: An Owner wants to take over materials procurement decisions and give instructions to the Contractor directly, skipping the Architect. Does this square with the Owner's responsibilities under SPP Document 202?
o: No — every instruction must instead pass through the specialist consultants
Yes — Owners are always free to bypass the Architect for efficiency's sake
No — Sec. 6.3 requires the Owner to route orders to the Contractor only through the Architect
Yes — but this is allowed only for Group 1 projects
n: Sec. 6.3 requires the Owner to route orders to the General Contractor only through the Architect, to avoid unreasonable delay and preserve the Architect's oversight role. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 6.3)

q: Architect Bautista's established office, per her letterhead, sits in Quezon City. The Owner requires her to render services at a site 80 kilometers away (straight-line/radial distance). What may be charged to the Owner under Sec. 7.4?
o: The full cost of temporarily relocating her office
Nothing extra — this distance still falls within the free-travel radius
A per diem, but only once the distance passes 100 kilometers, not 50
A per diem plus traveling and living expenses, since the site lies beyond the 50.0-kilometer threshold from her established office
n: Sec. 7.4 provides that a per diem plus traveling and living expenses is chargeable to the Owner whenever the Architect must perform services beyond 50.0 kilometers (air, straight-line or radial distance) from the office shown on the Architect's letterhead. At 80km, this threshold is exceeded. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.4)

q: In what respect does "Project Development Cost" (Sec. 7.18) go beyond "Project Construction Cost" (Sec. 7.17)?
o: Project Development Cost additionally folds in all professional fees, permits, clearances, utilities, site/lot acquisition cost, and cost of money, on top of the construction cost
Project Development Cost is always the smaller of the two figures
The two terms are simply different labels for the same amount
Project Development Cost leaves out construction cost entirely
n: Sec. 7.18 defines Project Development Cost as including the cost of construction PLUS all professional fees, permits, clearances, utilities, cost of acquiring the project site/lot, and cost of money - broader than the PCC alone. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.17, 7.18)

q: Which taxes on the Architect's project services, per Sec. 6.8, must the Owner pay?
o: Only local government taxes, never national ones
Only VAT; every other tax, income tax included, is the Owner's responsibility too
No taxes at all — these always fall to the Architect
All taxes government may impose because of the services rendered, VAT included, but NOT the Architect's own income tax
n: Sec. 6.8 requires the Owner to pay all reimbursable expenses and taxes including VAT that government may impose on the Architect as a result of services rendered, but excluding the Architect's income tax. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 6.8)

q: Under Sec. 7.5, who shoulders the cost of Contract Document sets beyond what has already been provided?
o: The Architect's professional liability insurer
The Architect, out of the basic professional fee
The Owner
The Contractor
n: Sec. 7.5 states the Owner shall pay the Architect for additional sets of Contract Documents. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.5)

q: Which item does Sec. 7.17 explicitly EXCLUDE from Project Construction Cost (PCC)?
o: The building's plumbing/sanitary and electrical fixtures
Mechanical equipment, elevators, and escalators
Fees for the Architect, the Engineer, the Specialist Consultants, or the salaries of construction inspectors
Fire protection, alarm, and communications/electronic systems
n: Sec. 7.17 explicitly states the PCC does not include any fees for the Architect, the Engineer, the Specialist Consultants, or the salaries of construction inspectors, while items like fixtures, equipment, elevators, and alarm/communication systems ARE part of the PCC. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.17)

q: Per Sec. 6.3, through what channel should the Owner send orders to the General Contractor?
o: Exclusively through the Project/Construction Manager
Only through the Architect
Through the specialist consultants
Directly to the Contractor at any time, bypassing the Architect
n: Sec. 6.3 states the Owner should issue orders to the General Contractor only through the Architect, to avoid unreasonable delay caused by miscommunication. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 6.3)

q: Under Secs. 6.6 and 6.7, besides the Architect's own fee, what other costs must the Owner arrange and cover?
o: Design/consulting services for acoustic, communication, electronic, and other specialty systems, plus legal, auditing, insurance, and counseling services as needed
The Architect's professional license renewal fees
The Architect's personal income tax
The PRC board examination fees of the Architect's staff
n: Sec. 6.6 requires the Owner to pay for design/consulting services on acoustic, communication, electronic and other specialty systems, and Sec. 6.7 requires the Owner to arrange and pay for legal, auditing, insurance, counseling and similar services. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 6.6, 6.7)

q: What general rule under Sec. 7.7 governs compensation whenever the Architect's work is abandoned or suspended, in whole or in part, at any stage — not only after Contract Documents?
o: The Architect must return whatever fees were already received
The Owner pays the Architect for services rendered, corresponding to the amount owed at the stage where suspension/abandonment occurred
The Owner pays only 10% of the fee no matter what stage was reached
The Architect forfeits every fee if the project never reaches construction
n: Sec. 7.7 states that if the Architect's work is abandoned or suspended in whole or in part, the Owner pays for the services rendered corresponding to the amount due at that stage. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.7)

q: During the Project Definition Phase, which two things does the Architect inform the Owner about, per Sec. 2.1?
o: The final construction cost and the contractor's profit margin
The zoning classification and the applicable real property tax
The building permit fee schedule and required bonds
The project's technical requirements and the corresponding professional fees
n: Sec. 2.1 states that in this phase the Architect informs the Owner of the technical requirements of the project and the concomitant professional fees. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 2.1)

q: Per Sec. 5.1, where is the Architect's Fee based on a Percentage (%) of Project Construction Cost (PCC) spelled out in detail?
o: In R.A. No. 9266 itself, Sec. 5
In the Architect's Guidelines
In SPP Document 203 only
In the National Building Code IRR
n: Sec. 5.1 states the Architect's Fee based on the PCC shall be detailed in the Architect's Guidelines. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.1)

q: A foreign Architect seeks to render architectural services on a Philippine project. Which specific requirement does Sec. 1.1.2 of SPP Document 202 impose?
o: Obtaining accreditation from the Bureau of Immigration only, with no local counterpart needed
Simply registering the project with the local government unit
Filing a notarized waiver with the PRC exempting compliance with Sec. 37 of R.A. No. 9266
Securing a Temporary/Special Permit (TSP) and a DOLE work permit, and working with a local counterpart Registered and Licensed Architect (RLA)
n: Sec. 1.1.2 requires a foreign architect to secure a TSP and work permit from DOLE and to work in collaboration with a local counterpart Architect who is a Registered and Licensed Architect (RLA) under Philippine law. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 1.1.2)

q: Given that the suspension ran 8 months (beyond the 6-month threshold), what is the adjusted fee for Architect Cruz's remaining works under Sec. 7.8, where P200,000 of the fee remained payable for the Construction Phase before construction — built in phases — was suspended for those 8 months?
n: Since the suspension (8 months) exceeds the 6-month threshold in Sec. 7.8, the fee for the remaining works is doubled: P200,000 x 2 = P400,000. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.8)

q: Per SPP Document 202, at what point does the Architect's regular design service work begin, and at what point does it end?
o: It begins upon issuance of the building permit and ends upon the final Certificate of Payment
It begins at the signing of the Owner-Architect agreement and ends at submission of the SPPCC
It begins at project inception, when the Owner outlines requirements, and ends only when the contractor turns the completed project over to the Owner
It begins at the Schematic Design Phase and ends at the Bidding Phase
n: Sec. 1.2.2 states the Architect's work starts at the inception of the project when the Owner outlines requirements, and ends only when the general contractor or builder turns over the completed project to the Owner. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 1.2.2)

q: A DTI-registered Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) firm in the Philippines wants to deliver architectural design services for a Philippine-based project on behalf of an overseas client. Is this permitted under Sec. 1.1.3?
o: Yes, so long as the firm is DTI- or SEC-registered, regardless of PRC registration
Yes, since the client is overseas, Philippine registration rules simply don't apply
No, unless the firm is a PRC-registered architectural firm meeting Sec. 37 of R.A. No. 9266 and its IRR
No, BPO/KPO firms may never render any architecture-related service under any circumstance
n: Sec. 1.1.3 states BPO/KPO firms are not authorized to provide architectural services for Philippine-soil projects unless they are PRC-registered architectural firms satisfying Sec. 37 of R.A. No. 9266. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 1.1.3)

q: If construction on that same project had instead been suspended for only four months, would Sec. 7.8's doubling rule kick in for the remaining fee?
o: No — doubling applies only once suspension exceeds six months; four months would not trigger it
Yes — any suspension at all automatically doubles the fee
No — a suspension of any length has no bearing on fees under this SPP
Yes — though the fee would be reduced rather than doubled
n: Sec. 7.8 only doubles the fee for remaining works when the suspension of construction exceeds six (6) months; a four-month suspension would not meet that threshold. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.8)

q: If the Owner wants the Architect to design movable/fixed cabinets and other architectural interior (AI) elements or site development plan (SDP) components, how is the Architect paid for this separate service under Sec. 7.10, and which other SPP Document supplies the compensation basis?
o: No extra compensation is ever allowed for these items
The Owner pays the Architect over and above the regular fee, based on Project Construction Cost as set out in SPP Document 203
It is compensated solely through the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses method
It comes free within the Group 4 classification fee
n: Sec. 7.10 provides that for AI, SDP, and similar items, the Owner pays the Architect in addition to the Architect's fee, with compensation based on the Project Construction Cost as provided under SPP Document 203. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.10)

q: Under the Per Diem, Honorarium Plus Reimbursable Expenses method (Sec. 5.5), which activity is specifically named as compensable this way?
o: Issuing the final Certificate of Payment
Preparing the Design Development documents
Conducting an ocular inspection of possible project sites
Preparing the complete Contract Documents
n: Sec. 5.5.2 lists "conducting ocular inspection of possible project sites" as one of the activities for which the Architect may be paid on a per diem and honorarium basis plus out-of-pocket expenses. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.5.2)

q: Per Sec. 5.2, between what values may the multiplier (M) used in the Direct Personnel Expenses method fall?
n: Sec. 5.2 states the multiplier ranges from 1.5 to 2.5 depending on the office set-up, overhead, experience of the Architect, and complexity of the project. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.2)

q: During the Contract Document Phase, how many sets of construction drawings and technical specifications does the Architect submit to the Owner for the building permit, per Sec. 2.4.3?
o: Seven (7) sets
Three (3) sets
Ten (10) sets
Five (5) sets
n: Sec. 2.4.3 requires the Architect to submit to the Owner seven (7) sets of all construction drawings and technical specifications for purposes of obtaining a building permit. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 2.4.3)

q: How does the Architect's role change between a competitive bid/procurement and a negotiated contract, per Secs. 2.5.2–2.5.3?
o: In negotiated contracts, the Owner alone handles all negotiations with no Architect involvement
In negotiated contracts, the Architect performs functions much like those in a competitive bid, but negotiates with a single Contractor rather than several bidders
In negotiated contracts, no Bid Documents are ever prepared
In competitive bids, the Architect's role ends once bidding opens
n: Sec. 2.5.3 states that for negotiated contracts, the Architect performs similar functions as in competitive bidding (Sec. 2.5.2) but negotiates with a single Contractor rather than multiple bidders. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 2.5.3)

q: SPP Document 202 forms part of the Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of which law, and which older document does it supersede?
o: P.D. 1096; supersedes the 1979 UAP Doc. 202
R.A. No. 9266; supersedes the 2004 UAP Doc. 202
R.A. No. 545; supersedes the 1979 UAP Doc. 203
R.A. No. 9266; supersedes the 1979 UAP Doc. 202
n: The document's header states it is part of the IRR of R.A. No. 9266 (The Architecture Act of 2004) and that it replaces the 1979 UAP Doc. 202. (Source: SPP Document 202, header)

q: Per Sec. 7.7, finishing the Detailed Design and Contract Documents Phase is treated as equivalent to what fraction of the Architect's total work — the basis on which Architect Cruz, who completed that entire phase for a project with a total agreed fee of P1,000,000 before the Owner scrapped the project, would be compensated?
o: One hundred percent (100%)
Seventy-five percent (75%)
Fifty percent (50%)
Ninety percent (90%)
n: Sec. 7.7 states that once the Architect has prepared all Detailed Design and Contract Documents, this is equivalent to ninety percent (90%) of the Architect's work. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.7)

q: Upon noticing or learning of anything that might jeopardize the project's successful completion, what must the Owner do under Sec. 6.9?
o: Withhold every payment until the Architect personally investigates
Terminate the Contractor's contract at once
Lodge a complaint with the PRBoA
Give the Architect prompt written notice
n: Sec. 6.9 requires the Owner to give prompt written notice to the Architect upon observing or becoming aware of anything that may impair successful project implementation. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 6.9)

q: What does Sec. 5.6 ("Mixed Methods of Compensation") say about how a project's compensation approach should be chosen?
o: Only one method may ever be used on a project, fixed at contract signing and never combined
More than one method of compensation may apply on a single project; each project should be examined to find the most appropriate approach
Mixed methods are barred under the IRR of R.A. No. 9266
Government projects must always combine Lump Sum with a Percentage of PCC
n: Sec. 5.6 provides that the SPP allows more than one method of compensation on a project, and each project should be examined to determine the most appropriate method. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.6)

q: Single-detached residences, single-attached or duplex homes, row-houses/shop-houses, small apartment houses, and townhouses fall under which classification Group?
o: Group 2
Group 9
Group 7
Group 4
n: Sec. 4.4 (Group 4) covers residences (single-detached, single-attached or duplex; row-houses or shop-houses), small apartment houses and townhouses. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 4.4)

q: Per Sec. 7.16, whose approval governs the size, design, and content of signboards the General Contractor, sub-contractors, jobbers, and dealers place at the project site during construction?
o: No approval is needed during construction
The Architect's
The Owner's building lessee's
The local government's building official alone
n: Sec. 7.16 states that all signboards placed at the project site during construction shall be approved by the Architect as to size, design and contents. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.16)

q: An Owner asks the Architect to design built-in cabinets, special fittings, screens, counters, and architectural interiors, along with development planning. Which Group covers this?
o: Group 8
Group 10
Group 1
Group 4
n: Sec. 4.8 (Group 8) covers projects involving extensive detail such as built-in components/elements, built-in equipment, special fittings, screens, counters, architectural interiors (AI), and development planning and/or design. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 4.8)

q: If the Owner orders design changes after the Architect's outputs have already been approved, who bears the cost of the resulting additional professional services under Sec. 7.6?
o: The cost is split automatically and equally between Owner and Architect
The Architect absorbs every cost of an Owner-initiated change
The Owner, who must pay the Architect for the extra time, resources/drafting, or other office expenses involved
The Contractor, since changes affect the construction schedule
n: Sec. 7.6 states that if the Architect renders additional services due to changes ordered by the Owner after approval of outputs, the Owner shall pay the Architect for extra time, resources/drafting, or other office expenses. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.6)

q: What distinguishes Group 6 from Group 7 in SPP Document 202's project classification?
o: Group 6 covers alterations, while Group 7 covers new construction only
Group 6 covers residences only, while Group 7 covers commercial buildings only

Group 6 covers plans/Contract Documents reused for repetitive construction of similar buildings (not necessarily on one site), while Group 7 specifically means a housing project on a single site using one set of plans
Group 6 and Group 7 have identical scope
n: Sec. 4.6 (Group 6) covers projects where plans/Contract Documents are re-used for repetitive construction of similar buildings without amending drawings/specifications, while Sec. 4.7 (Group 7) is the specific case of a housing project on a single site with one set of plans. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 4.6, 4.7)

q: Under Sec. 7.8, what becomes of the fee for Architect Cruz's remaining works — where P200,000 stayed payable for the Construction Phase — once construction suspension (built as it was in phases) stretches past six months?
o: The fee for the remaining works is cut in half
The fee for the remaining works is doubled
The Architect forfeits the remaining fee outright
The fee stays exactly as originally set, whatever the suspension's length
n: Sec. 7.8 provides that when suspension of construction exceeds a period of six (6) months, the fee for the remaining works shall be doubled. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.8)

q: Per Sec. 1.1.4, what may cause the Architect's outputs listed under this SPP to be expanded or increased?
o: Nothing — the outputs stay fixed regardless of the project or the Architect
The project's requirements, or the Architect's experience, capabilities, and specialization(s)
Only a special Board resolution issued for that specific project
Only when project cost exceeds P100 million
n: Sec. 1.1.4 provides that the Architect's outputs may be expanded or increased depending on the project requirements or the Architect's experience, capabilities and specialization/s. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 1.1.4)

q: Under Sec. 4, on what basis is professional architectural work sorted into Groups?
o: The building's number of storeys alone
The Owner's nationality
The project's total floor area alone
The degree of complexity and creative skill needed to satisfy the Client's requirements within technical, functional, economic, and aesthetic constraints
n: Sec. 4 states architectural work is classified according to the degree of complexity and creative skill required to meet the Client's requirements within technical, functional, economic, and aesthetic constraints. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 4)

q: Applying the 90% rule of Sec. 7.7, how much compensation is Architect Cruz owed for the abandoned project, given his total agreed fee of P1,000,000 after finishing the entire Contract Documents phase?
n: Since the Owner failed to implement the plans/documents after the Contract Documents Phase was completed (equivalent to 90% of the work), the Architect is entitled to 90% of the agreed fee: P1,000,000 x 0.90 = P900,000. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.7)

q: A hospital, a hotel, and an airport terminal are being classified under SPP Document 202. Which Group fits?
o: Group 3 — buildings of exceptional character and complexity of plan/design
Group 2 — buildings of moderate complexity
Group 9 — alterations and renovations
Group 1 — buildings of the simplest utilization
n: Sec. 4.3 (Group 3) lists Hospitals & Medical Buildings, Hotels, and Airports/Terminals among buildings of exceptional character and complexity. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 4.3)

q: If parts of a building go up in separate periods — stretching the construction timeline and the Architect's service burden — what does Sec. 7.8 provide for Construction Phase charges?
o: Charges for services rendered during the Construction Phase are adjusted proportionately
Only the Contractor's charges are adjusted, never the Architect's
Charges stay fixed at the original contract amount, with no adjustment
The Architect must absorb the added burden with no extra pay
n: Sec. 7.8 states that if portions of the building are erected at different periods, increasing construction period and the Architect's burden of services, charges for Construction Phase services shall be adjusted proportionately. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.8)

q: Although SPP Document 202 speaks specifically to the individual professional practice of the Architect as a natural person, to what else may it also apply?
o: Engineering firms with no architect-in-charge
Only foreign architecture firms operating abroad
Only government agencies that employ architects
The Architect's group practice as part of a DTI-registered sole proprietorship or an SEC-registered partnership/corporation
n: Sec. 1.1.1 extends applicability to the Architect's "group practice" as part of a juridical entity (DTI-registered sole proprietorship or SEC-registered partnership/corporation), subject to full compliance with Sec. 37 of R.A. No. 9266. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 1.1.1)

q: If the Owner supplies materials for the project below their market cost, how are that material's cost and its installation labor treated when computing the PCC under Sec. 7.17?
o: They are nonetheless computed on the basis of current, fair market value
They are excluded from the PCC entirely, since the Owner supplied them
They are computed at the below-market price the Owner actually paid
They are computed at zero cost, since no cash changed hands
n: Sec. 7.17 provides that even if materials/labor are furnished by the Owner below market cost, they shall nonetheless be computed on the basis of current (fair market value) costs for PCC purposes. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.17)

q: In ordinary practice, what role does the Architect occupy relative to the Owner, Client, or Proponent?
o: The Contractor's exclusive agent
A co-owner of the finished structure
An independent regulator of the project
The Owner's/Client's/Proponent's Adviser and/or Representative
n: Sec. 1.2.1 states that in regular practice, the Architect acts as the Owner's/Client's/Proponent's Adviser and/or Representative, translating the Owner's needs into spaces and forms. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 1.2.1)

q: The Schematic Design Phase (Sec. 2.2) calls for preparing what kind of studies, and produces what cost-related deliverable?
o: Schematic design studies leading to conceptual plans, culminating in a Statement of the Probable Project Construction Cost (SPPCC)
Bid abstracts, culminating in a notice of award
As-built drawings, culminating in a warranty schedule
Detailed structural computations, culminating in a final bill of quantities
n: Sec. 2.2 describes schematic design studies leading to conceptual plans, and Sec. 2.2.3 has the Architect submit a Statement of the Probable Project Construction Cost (SPPCC) based on current cost parameters. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 2.2, 2.2.3)

q: A client simply asks an Architect for a technical opinion and clarification on an architectural matter, with no design or drawing output involved. Which Group covers this?
o: Group 8 — extensive detail projects
This falls outside every Group and cannot be compensated
Group 1 — simplest utilization buildings
Group 10 — where the Architect renders opinion or gives advice, clarification, or explanation on technical matters
n: Sec. 4.10 (Group 10) covers engagements where the Architect is engaged to render opinion or give advice, clarifications, or explanation on technical matters pertaining to architectural works. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 4.10)

q: Per Sec. 7.13, is the Architect's Fee treated as gross or net, and who covers applicable government taxes (other than income tax) arising from the Architect's services?
o: Fees under this SPP are always tax-exempt
A net amount, with all taxes, income tax included, paid by the Owner
A gross amount already inclusive of all taxes, paid by the Architect
A net amount; national and/or local government taxes (excluding income tax) are paid by the Owner
n: Sec. 7.13 states the Architect's Fee is a net amount, and any tax (exclusive of income tax) imposed on the Architect due to the project's services shall be paid by the Owner. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.13)

q: For what kind of projects is the Lump Sum or Fixed Fee method of compensation (Sec. 5.4) noted as especially fitting, and why?
o: Group 10 opinion/advisory engagements only
Foreign-funded projects only, owing to currency conversion issues
Government projects, since they involve more paperwork and time-consuming effort
Private residential projects, since owners prefer simplicity
n: Sec. 5.4 states this method may be applied to government projects since they entail more paper work and time-consuming efforts. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.4)

q: Per Sec. 7.15, what must the Owner give the Architect while construction is ongoing and once it is complete?
o: Nothing — compiling cost records is solely the Architect's job
A notarized waiver releasing the Architect from liability
A copy of the Contractor's tax returns
A copy of the records/summary of expenses, labor, services, materials, equipment, and fixtures used in construction
n: Sec. 7.15 requires the Owner to furnish the Architect a copy of expense records during construction, and a summary of all cost of labor, services, materials, equipment and fixtures upon completion. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.15)

q: Under Sec. 7.14 and Sec. 33 of R.A. No. 9266, who retains ownership of the designs, drawings, models, specifications, and other contract documents the Architect prepares and seals, even if the work never gets built?
o: They automatically become the Owner's exclusive property upon signing and sealing
They fall into the public domain, usable by anyone
Ownership passes to the Contractor at groundbreaking
They remain the intellectual property and documents of the Architect
n: Sec. 7.14 states these instruments of service are the intellectual property and documents of the Architect (Sec. 33, R.A. No. 9266), whether or not the work is executed, and may not be reproduced/used elsewhere without a written agreement with the Architect. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.14)

q: During the Construction Phase, must the Architect provide continuous 8-hour on-site supervision, per Sec. 2.6.3?
o: No supervision whatsoever is required of the Architect during construction
Yes, but only for projects classified under Group 3
No — the Architect conducts periodic site visits and need not render exhaustive or continuous 8-hour on-site supervision
Yes, full-time 8-hour supervision by the Architect personally is always mandatory
n: Sec. 2.6.3 states the Architect makes periodic site visits and shall not be required to make exhaustive or continuous 8-hour on-site supervision, nor be held responsible for the Contractor's failure to follow the Contract Documents. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 2.6.3)

q: Beyond plans, elevations, sections, and outline specifications, what else does the Architect prepare during the Design Development Phase, per Sec. 2.3?
o: The final building permit and occupancy permit
A signed construction contract with the winning bidder
A diagrammatic layout of construction systems and an updated SPPCC
The notice to proceed and the performance bond
n: Sec. 2.3.3-2.3.4 require a diagrammatic layout of construction systems and an updated SPPCC for submission to the Owner during the Design Development Phase. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 2.3.3, 2.3.4)

q: An Owner wants full-time (8-hour) construction supervision, beyond the Architect's usual periodic site visits. What does Sec. 2.6.5 say about this?
o: The Architect must personally provide it at no extra cost as part of regular design services
This kind of service is legally barred under R.A. No. 9266
A separate full-time supervisor is hired as agreed by Owner and Architect, compensated separately under the applicable SPP Document on Full-Time Supervision
The Contractor must supply this supervisor at no charge
n: Sec. 2.6.5 provides that if more extensive inspection or full-time supervision is required, a separate full-time supervisor is hired and paid subject to conditions in the SPP Document on Full-Time Supervision, with fees covered separately. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 2.6.5)

q: Under Sec. 3, in what two ways may an Architect, as Lead Professional, contract with the Owner alongside other engineering/allied professionals?
o: A single contract with sub-consultancy contracts between the Architect and the other professionals, OR separate contracts executed directly between the Owner and each professional
Only through contracts routed exclusively via the general contractor
Only through a government-mediated procurement contract
Only through one joint-and-several contract binding all professionals equally
n: Sec. 3.1 and 3.2 describe (1) a single contract between Architect and Owner with sub-consultancy contracts, and (2) separate contracts between the Owner and each of the Architect and the engineering/allied professionals. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 3.1, 3.2)

q: Under Sec. 5.2's formula, what does the variable "R" stand for, and what example of an R-includable expense is given?
o: The Architect's own hourly rate
The Registered Licensed Professional's income tax due
Retention money withheld from the Contractor
Reimbursable expenses, such as transportation/housing/living allowance for consultants and technical staff assigned beyond 100 km from the Architect's area of operation
n: The formula section defines R as reimbursable expenses such as transportation, per diem, housing and living allowance of consultants and technical staff assigned to places over 100km from the Architect's area of operation, plus items like extra printing costs, long-distance calls, tests, licenses, fees and taxes. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.2 (Formula, definition of R))

q: Per Sec. 7.12, is the Architect professionally responsible for inaccuracies in an SPPCC or Cost Estimate he submitted?
o: No, unless glaring errors or discrepancies are clearly evident, since the Architect has no control over labor/material costs or competitive-bidding factors
Yes — the Architect absolutely guarantees the accuracy of every cost estimate
No, the Architect bears no responsibility under any circumstance, even for glaring errors
Yes, but only for Group 1 and Group 2 projects
n: Sec. 7.12 states an SPPCC/Cost Estimate can attain only a certain degree of accuracy, and the Architect does not assume professional responsibility for such estimates unless glaring errors or discrepancies are clearly evident. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.12)

q: Per Sec. 1.1.2, Board resolutions may require a foreign architect to work alongside which of the following?
o: A licensed foreign notary public
A local counterpart Civil Engineer only
A representative of the Department of Foreign Affairs
A local counterpart Architect
n: Sec. 1.1.2 notes that Board resolutions may call for a "local counterpart Architect" to work with any foreign architect offering services in the Philippines. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 1.1.2)

q: Schools, churches, shopping centers, and office buildings belong to which Group?
o: Group 1 — buildings of simplest utilization
Group 2 — buildings of moderate complexity of plan/design
Group 5 — monumental buildings
Group 4 — residences
n: Sec. 4.2 (Group 2) lists Schools, Churches and Religious Facilities, Shopping Centers, and Office Buildings among buildings of moderate complexity of plan/design. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 4.2)

q: If a scale model, 3D model, or walk-through presentation of the Architect's design is needed (Sec. 7.3), how is its cost treated?
o: It is never allowed under SPP Document 202
It is recommended by the Architect for Owner approval, paid separately by the Owner, and subject to a coordination fee to the Architect
It is always included free within the basic professional fee
It is billed directly to the Contractor as a construction cost
n: Sec. 7.3 treats scale models, 3D models and walk-thru presentations the same way as Sec. 7.2's other services - recommended by the Architect, paid separately by the Owner, subject to a coordination fee. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.3)

q: Which output specifically comes out of the END of the Project Definition Phase, per Sec. 2.1.4?
o: The complete Contract Documents
An initial statement of probable construction cost
The final Certificate of Payment
The Design Development documents
n: Sec. 2.1.4 states that in the Project Definition Phase, the Architect prepares an initial statement of probable construction cost. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 2.1.4)

q: Years after completion, a Group 2 office building undergoes a major renovation, retrofit, and expansion. How is this project classified under Sec. 4.9?
o: It no longer falls under any classification in this SPP
Group 9 — alterations, renovations, rehabilitations, retrofit, and expansion/additions to existing buildings belonging to Groups 1 to 5
Group 6, since the original plans are being reused
It automatically reverts to Group 1
n: Sec. 4.9 (Group 9) covers alterations, renovations, rehabilitations, retrofit and expansion/additions to existing buildings belonging to Groups 1 to 5. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 4.9)

q: Per Sec. 7.11, when no Project/Construction Manager is on site, whose technical control and supervision governs the full-time construction supervisor?
o: The General Contractor's
The Owner's, bypassing the Architect
The specialist consultants', collectively
The Architect's
n: Sec. 7.11 states that if no Project/Construction Manager is present, the full-time construction supervisor is under the technical control and supervision of the Architect, and reports periodically to Owner and Architect. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 7.11)

q: Which of the following does SPP Document 202 (2010 Standards of Professional Practice) govern?
o: The Code of Ethical Conduct for Architects
Regular Design Services of the Architect
Specialized Architectural Services only
Continuing Professional Development requirements
n: SPP Document 202 is titled "Standard of Professional Practice on Regular Design Services" and covers the scope of services, classification of projects, and compensation methods for an Architect's regular design work. (Source: SPP Document 202, Title)

q: At the outset of a commission compensated under the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses method, what must the Architect disclose to the Client, per Sec. 5.2?
o: Only the total lump-sum estimate, with no rate breakdown
Nothing — rates may be disclosed only once the project is finished
The rate of professionals/personnel to be assigned and the multiplier to apply, before agreeing to this method
Only the multiplier, never the individual rates
n: Sec. 5.2 requires the Architect to make known to the Client, at the start of the commission, the rate of professionals/personnel assigned to the project and the multiplier to be applied, before agreeing on this method. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.2)

q: Museums, expositions and fair buildings, and mausoleums/memorials/monuments fall under which classification Group?
o: Group 3 — buildings of exceptional character
Group 5 — monumental buildings and other facilities
Group 8 — projects with extensive detail
Group 10 — opinion or advice
n: Sec. 4.5 (Group 5) covers monumental buildings and other facilities, including Exposition & Fair Buildings and Mausoleums, Memorials & Monuments. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 4.5)

q: A developer plans to build 40 identical row houses on one site using a single set of plans, specifications, and related documents. Which classification Group most precisely fits this?
o: Group 6 — repetitive construction of similar buildings without amending drawings
Group 4 — residences
Group 9 — alterations and renovations
Group 7 — a Housing Project involving several residential units on a single site using one (1) set of plans/design
n: Sec. 4.7 (Group 7) specifically describes a Housing Project involving construction of several residential units on a single site using one (1) set of plans/design, specifications, and related documents. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 4.7)

q: Applying the agreed 2.0 multiplier, what is Architect Reyes's Fee for this engagement?
n: Fee = Direct Cost x M = P62,000 x 2.0 = P124,000. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.2 (Formula: Fee = Direct Cost x M))
scenario: Architect Reyes takes on a small renovation job — non-creative, cost-based work — under the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses method (SPP Doc. 202, Sec. 5.2). Her own billing rate is P800/hour across 40 logged hours; her Consultant bills P600/hour for 20 hours; and her Technical Staff bills P300/hour for 60 hours. The parties settle on a multiplier (M) of 2.0 to cover overhead and profit, and reimbursable expenses (R) for the whole engagement come to P15,000.

q: A junior architect tells a client, "Since the design is creative work, I'll just bill you my hourly design time times an overhead factor." Does this square with SPP Document 202's Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses method?
o: No — Sec. 5.2 restricts this cost-based method to non-creative work only; the value of creative design work cannot be measured by time spent
No — this method may never apply to any type of work under any SPP
Yes — this method is meant specifically and only for creative design work
Yes — provided the multiplier used exceeds 2.5
n: Sec. 5.2 expressly limits the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses method to non-creative, cost-based work, since the value of creative design cannot be measured by hours spent. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.2)

q: What Total Cost of Service should be billed to the Client here?
n: Total Cost of Service = Fee + R = P124,000 + P15,000 = P139,000. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.2 (Formula: Total Cost of Service = Fee + R))
scenario: Architect Reyes takes on a small renovation job — non-creative, cost-based work — under the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses method (SPP Doc. 202, Sec. 5.2). Her own billing rate is P800/hour across 40 logged hours; her Consultant bills P600/hour for 20 hours; and her Technical Staff bills P300/hour for 60 hours. The parties settle on a multiplier (M) of 2.0 to cover overhead and profit, and reimbursable expenses (R) for the whole engagement come to P15,000.

q: Which compensation method is described as commonly used where a continuing relationship spans a series of Projects, fixing a sum above and beyond reimbursement for technical time and overhead?
o: Professional Fee Plus Expenses (Sec. 5.3)
Per Diem, Honorarium Plus Reimbursable Expenses (Sec. 5.5)
Percentage of Project Construction Cost (Sec. 5.1)
Lump Sum or Fixed Fee (Sec. 5.4)
n: Sec. 5.3 describes Professional Fee Plus Expenses as frequently used in continuing relationships involving a series of projects, establishing a fixed sum above reimbursement for technical time and overhead. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.3)

q: Within SPP Document 202, the acronym SPPCC expands to:
o: Standard Practice for Project Cost Control
Statement of the Probable Project Construction Cost
Summary of Prior Project Construction Contracts
Schedule of Prescribed Professional Compensation and Charges
n: Sec. 2.2.3 defines SPPCC as the Statement of the Probable Project Construction Cost, submitted based on current cost parameters. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 2.2.3)

q: Under either contracting arrangement described in Sec. 3, what becomes of each involved State-regulated professional's professional responsibilities and civil liabilities?
o: They are extinguished once the building permit is issued
They merge automatically under the Architect's sole liability
They stay separate; the Architect does not take on the responsibilities and liabilities of the other Registered and Licensed Professionals (RLPs)
They pass entirely to the Owner
n: Sec. 3 states that in both contracting arrangements, professional responsibilities and civil liabilities of each State-regulated professional remain separate, and the Architect does not assume the responsibilities/liabilities of other RLPs. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 3)

q: What is the Direct Cost (AN + CN + TN) of this engagement?
n: Direct cost = AN + CN + TN = (800x40) + (600x20) + (300x60) = 32,000 + 12,000 + 18,000 = P62,000. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 5.2 (Formula: Direct cost = AN + CN + TN))
scenario: Architect Reyes takes on a small renovation job — non-creative, cost-based work — under the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses method (SPP Doc. 202, Sec. 5.2). Her own billing rate is P800/hour across 40 logged hours; her Consultant bills P600/hour for 20 hours; and her Technical Staff bills P300/hour for 60 hours. The parties settle on a multiplier (M) of 2.0 to cover overhead and profit, and reimbursable expenses (R) for the whole engagement come to P15,000.

q: What effect does a Certificate for Payment issued by the Architect have, under Sec. 2.6.4?
o: It guarantees the Contractor's workmanship will be defect-free for the building's entire life
It transfers ownership of the building to the Contractor
It certifies to the Client that the work has progressed to the indicated stage and, to the Architect's best knowledge, conforms to the Contract Documents
It automatically extends the Contractor's performance bond
n: Sec. 2.6.4 states these Certificates constitute a certification to the Client that work has progressed to the indicated stage and, to the Architect's best knowledge, that the Contractor's work quality conforms to the Contract Documents. (Source: SPP Document 202, Sec. 2.6.4)
